documents.title: An external view
documents.plain: This small context interprets the article’s system boundaries. It omits internal storage and replication details.

ste.text: This diagram shows the system and its users. It does not show internal parts.

documents.title: Git user
documents.plain: Developers use Git operations to exchange repository changes. The person is a context abstraction.

ste.text: The developer sends and receives repository changes.

documents.title: Continuity
documents.plain: Cursor describes Continuity as a Git storage system. Its write-ahead log is the source of truth.

ste.text: Continuity stores repository changes in a write-ahead log.

documents.title: Object storage
documents.plain: The article identifies S3 as the production object store. The context shows this as an external dependency.

ste.text: The object store holds the write-ahead log.

documents.title: Logical container view
documents.plain: This is an inferred C4 decomposition of the article’s responsibilities. A logical Continuity server uses a local Git repository and the external S3 WAL. It does not claim separate deployable services, host counts, or a production topology.

ste.text: This view shows logical parts. The server uses a local Git repository and S3 storage. The boundaries are inferred.

documents.title: Continuity server (inferred boundary)
documents.plain: The article describes servers preparing reference transactions and accessing the WAL. This diagram groups those responsibilities into one inferred application container.

ste.text: The server prepares reference transactions and uses the WAL. This application boundary is inferred.

documents.title: Local Git repository
documents.plain: The article describes a normal Git repository on NVMe as a warm cache. The datastore container is a logical abstraction; the article does not describe it as a separate service.

ste.text: The local Git repository acts as a cache. The datastore boundary is inferred.

documents.title: Replica role (inferred)
documents.plain: This logical role checks freshness before serving. Gossip helps catch-up; it is not a correctness requirement.

ste.text: Check freshness before you serve a read. Gossip helps the replica.

documents.title: Push: durable publication
documents.plain: Original abstraction: WAL persistence and local preparation precede CAS publication. Branches keep independent order; boundaries are inferred.

ste.text: Store the WAL entry. Prepare the references. Publish the index. Then acknowledge the push.

documents.title: Read: freshness already matches
documents.plain: A conditional freshness check guards serving. This successful 304 path is separate from catch-up.

ste.text: Check freshness. If the index is unchanged, serve the read.

documents.title: Read: catch up before serving
documents.plain: The 200 path receives the new index and catches up before serving. It does not depend on gossip delivery.

ste.text: Get the new index. Get missing data. Catch up before you serve the read.

documents.title: Compaction: reuse compacted packs
documents.plain: Only the primary compacts; replicas follow the WAL and reuse the result. Role boundaries are inferred.

ste.text: The primary compacts the data. The replica gets the compacted packs.

documents.title: Gossip: optional catch-up notification
documents.plain: Gossip accelerates catch-up. Lost notifications do not remove conditional freshness checks on read paths.

ste.text: Gossip helps catch-up. A read still needs a freshness check.

documents.title: Illustrative deployment
documents.plain: This topology is hypothetical. It demonstrates nested hosts, distinct server replicas, a cache, and durable storage. The article supports the logical roles and S3 durability. It does not establish the host count, regions, replica placement, process boundaries, or implementation language shown here. Collapsing a host hides its descendants and their relationships; no ancestor relationship is invented.
